blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,θ)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.

blocks.en:
Localizing a moving sensor against a 2D floor plan is attractive: floor
plans already exist, are compact, and avoid dense 3D mapping. Recent systems
such as F3Loc [ 7 ] and UnLoc [ 30 ] pair learned
per-column depth with a dense Bayes-filter recursion over an ( x , y , θ ) (x,y,\theta) grid—robust, but the posterior is large and persistent, and the design
is tied to one depth front-end.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
F3Loc [ 7 ] and UnLoc [ 30 ] are the closest
learned-depth baselines on Gibson. Both pair learned per-column depth
predictions with a classical dense recursive Bayes filter over ( x , y , θ ) (x,y,\theta) ; UnLoc adds Depth-Anything-v2 [ 32 ] depth, aleatoric ray uncertainty, and offline SE(2) refinement. Earlier work includes learned
layout retrieval [ 14 , 13 ] , latent floor-plan
matching [ 20 ] , monocular layout filtering [ 4 ] , and
RGB-D floor-plan localization [ 29 ] . Z-FLoc with
MapAnything [ 17 ] uses completed multiview depth and
batched geometric matching [ 27 ] , so
we compare to it only in the batched regime. PadLoc instead keeps a sparse
translation posterior, replaces dense orientation filtering with dominant
wall-orientation candidates, and evaluates the same back-end under matched
learned-depth front-ends.

blocks.en:
Padfield [ 24 ] introduced Fourier-domain masked NCC. We
adapt it to weighted masks (§ 3.3 ), with a building-interior
mask and an observed-support mask: observed
free space penalizes overlapping reference walls, while unobserved cells drop
out. The contribution is to expose the full translation response as a
multi-hypothesis posterior for temporal decoding. Similar sparse
representations appear in mixture filters and factor-graph
smoothers [ 22 , 16 ] , but our observations are
local maxima of a masked correlation surface. The orientation prior is
classical as well: Manhattan-world and dominant-direction assumptions are
standard in indoor layout estimation [ 8 ] and scan
matching [ 18 , 23 ] . PadLoc uses that prior
to remove the dense θ \theta axis while retaining multiple directed
candidates.

blocks.en:
Very short sparse-depth trajectories still suffer directed heading
ambiguity ( 14 14 – 29 % 29\% wrong-family chunks at T = 15 T{=}15 : the free-space wedge is
too small to reject the 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} mirror). Under high drift the filter can stay locked on a wrong basin; the consensus
peak-to-sidelobe ratio (PSR) flags this but does not relocalize.
The method assumes stable wall structure; furniture, renovations, or
long-term change make map quality decisive. The five Hilti sessions split
into three regimes: matching walls, as-built walls where free space
carries, and clutter where wall isolation recovers structure
(§ 4.5 ). No variant is best on every session, and we do not
evaluate a selector between them. Fixed parameters were set on Gibson; Bonn modularity
and lag sweeps concentrate on static_0 at small n n .

blocks.en: Appendix D Confidence thresholding versus intensity weighting

blocks.en:
The main paper (§3) treats depth uncertainty as membership rather than intensity — for b ^ \hat{b} the discriminative control is which
cells participate in the masked NCC, not how strongly each is weighted. The
mask does carry one fixed geometric weight (wall hits over
observed-free cells, §3), and the overlap mass α w b \alpha_{w}^{b} weights the
cross-heading selection; what the back-end field does not use is a
per-cell depth-confidence weight. Here we report the ablation that
motivates that membership choice.

confidence, down-weighting free-space cells with large aleatoric

blocks.en:
The main paper’s controlled T T -sweep holds UnLoc’s 10 cm 10\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} DeSDF grid so that no resolution asymmetry confounds the comparison. PadLoc’s
matching cell is, however, a free knob—independent of the front-end and bounded

motion covariance in metres (main-paper Eq. (5)). Differences therefore
cannot be attributed to sampling density or quantization alone.

cost rises in steps, one per power-of-two FFT size. the phone.
